species.hab: Gardens, meadows, woodland edges, parks. Very common throughout Sjælland. Adults hibernate in buildings and sheds.
feat: Large distinctive eyespots on all four wings — unmistakable
Upperside rich red-brown with blue, yellow and black eyespots
Underside almost black — superb camouflage when wings closed
Wingspan 50–65 mm
Makes a hissing sound by rubbing wings together when disturbed
species.season: Adults emerge from hibernation March–April, fly until June. New generation July–September, then hibernates. Often found indoors in autumn.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, roadsides, parks. One of the commonest Danish butterflies. Larvae feed on stinging nettles.
feat: Orange-red wings with black, yellow and blue markings
Row of blue half-moon spots along outer wing margins
Underside dark mottled brown — cryptic when closed
Wingspan 40–52 mm
Often basks with wings spread open on sunny surfaces
species.season: Adults from hibernation March–May. New generation June–September. Hibernates in buildings, often in clusters.

conf.d: Peacock is larger with prominent circular eyespots, not the mosaic pattern of the tortoiseshell.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, orchards, woodland edges. Common on Sjælland. Migratory — arrives from southern Europe each spring.
feat: Velvety black wings with striking red-orange bands and white spots
Forewings have a diagonal red band; hindwings have a red marginal band
Underside beautifully marbled in dark browns, blues and cream
Wingspan 55–65 mm
Attracted to rotting fruit, ivy flowers and buddleia
species.season: Migrants arrive May–June. Most abundant August–October on fallen fruit and ivy. Some attempt to overwinter but rarely survive Danish winters.

conf.d: Painted lady is paler orange-brown overall with no solid red bands, and has a more washed-out, mottled appearance.

species.hab: Open areas, meadows, gardens, roadsides. Migratory — numbers vary hugely year to year. Some years almost absent, others in millions.
feat: Orange-brown wings with black spots and white patches near wingtips
More delicate and paler than Red Admiral
Underside hindwing has intricate pattern of eye-like spots
Wingspan 50–60 mm
Fast, direct flight; migrates thousands of kilometres from North Africa
species.season: Arrives May–June in variable numbers. Breeds here; new generation August–September. Mass migration years are spectacular events.

conf.d: Red Admiral has bold red bands on black, much stronger contrast than the painted lady's softer patterning.

species.hab: Woodland rides, hedgerows, gardens. Common on Sjælland. One of the longest-lived butterflies (10–11 months as adult).
feat: Male: bright sulphur-yellow wings — unmistakable in flight
Female: pale greenish-white, easily mistaken for a white butterfly
Uniquely leaf-shaped wings with pointed tips
Single orange spot centre of each wing
Wingspan 52–60 mm
species.season: One of the first butterflies in spring (February–March from hibernation). Flies until June, then new adults from July, hibernating from September. Lives almost a full year.

conf.d: Large white has rounded (not pointed) wing tips, black wing tips, and flies with a fluttery (not gliding) action.

species.hab: Gardens, allotments, farmland, parks. Very common. The classic 'cabbage white'. Larvae are a significant garden pest.
feat: White wings with black tips on forewing — reaches along the wing edge
Female has two additional black spots on forewing and one on hindwing
Underside yellowish-green with faint grey scaling
Wingspan 55–65 mm — largest of the common whites
Gregarious caterpillars — black and yellow, strongly patterned
species.season: Two generations: April–June and July–September. Often seen around vegetable gardens. Can be abundant.

conf.d: Small white is noticeably smaller, has less extensive black at wingtips, and single (not gregarious) caterpillars.

species.hab: Gardens, farmland, meadows, parks. Very common everywhere. Often the most abundant butterfly.
feat: White wings with small black spots and greyish (not extensive black) wingtips
Smaller and daintier than Large White
Underside hindwing pale yellowish
Wingspan 40–50 mm
Solitary green caterpillar — less obvious pest than Large White
species.season: Multiple generations March–October. Can be seen on almost any sunny day in summer. Very common.

conf.d: Large white is distinctly bigger with much more extensive black at the wingtips.

species.hab: Hedgerows, damp meadows, woodland rides, gardens. Common spring butterfly on Sjælland.
feat: Male: white with bright orange patches on wingtips — very distinctive
Female: white with greyish wingtips, no orange — easily mistaken for a white
Underside hindwing mottled green and white (moss-like camouflage)
Wingspan 38–48 mm
Fluttering flight along hedgerows and lanes
species.season: Single generation: April–June. One of the defining spring butterflies. Females easily overlooked.

conf.d: Female orange tips can be confused with small whites, but look at the underside hindwing — mottled green in orange tip, plain yellowish in small white.

species.hab: Grassland, meadows, dunes, roadsides, parks. Fairly common on Sjælland where habitat exists.
feat: Male: bright violet-blue upperside with thin white fringe
Female: brown with variable blue at wing bases and orange marginal spots
Underside pale grey-beige with black spots ringed in white, plus orange marginal spots
Wingspan 28–36 mm — small butterfly
Caterpillars feed on bird's-foot trefoil and clovers
species.season: Two generations: May–June and July–September. Found in flowery grassland. Numbers declining with habitat loss.

conf.d: Holly blue has plain pale blue underside with just scattered small black dots, no orange spots. Flies around shrubs/trees, not grassland.

species.hab: Meadows, grassland, roadsides, woodland rides, gardens. One of the commonest Danish butterflies in summer.
feat: Brown wings with a single small eyespot (with white pupil) near forewing tip
Female larger and more orange on forewings than male
Underside hindwing grey-brown with wavy line
Wingspan 40–55 mm
Characteristic bobbing, lazy flight low over grass
species.season: Single generation: June–September. The dominant butterfly of grassy habitats in midsummer. Very abundant.

conf.d: Ringlet is darker chocolate-brown with multiple small eyespots (not just one) and prefers shadier habitats.

species.hab: Woodland edges, shady lanes, damp meadows, hedgerows. Common on Sjælland.
feat: Uniform dark chocolate-brown wings
Underside has 2–5 prominent eyespots with yellow rings — key feature
Upperside often appears almost black in flight
Wingspan 40–48 mm
Prefers shadier, damper habitats than Meadow Brown
species.season: Single generation: June–August. Flies in shady rides and along hedgerows, often in dappled light.

conf.d: Meadow brown is paler brown, has orange patches (especially females), only one eyespot, and prefers open sunny grassland.

species.hab: Woodland, shady lanes, hedgerows, mature gardens with trees. Common on Sjælland.
feat: Dark brown wings with cream or pale yellow dappled spots
Single eyespot near tip of forewing, three on underside hindwing
Underside hindwing beautifully marbled grey-brown
Wingspan 38–45 mm
Males territorial — defend patches of sunlight on the woodland floor
species.season: Multiple generations April–October. Flies in dappled woodland light. Males sit on sunlit leaves and chase off rivals.

species.hab: Woodland edges, hedgerows, gardens. Fairly common on Sjælland. Increasing in recent decades.
feat: Ragged, deeply scalloped wing edges — unlike any other Danish butterfly
Orange-brown upperside with dark spots
Underside dark brown with a small white comma-shaped mark — the namesake
Wingspan 42–50 mm
When closed, looks exactly like a dead leaf
species.season: Adults from hibernation March–April, new generation July–September. Superb dead-leaf camouflage in winter roosts.

conf.d: Tortoiseshell has smooth (not ragged) wing edges, blue marginal spots, and brighter orange coloration.

species.hab: Flower-rich meadows, coastal grassland, roadsides. Locally common on Sjælland.
feat: Glossy blue-black forewings with 6 bright red spots (3 pairs)
Hindwings red with narrow dark border
Clubbed antennae (not feathered) — unusual for a moth
Wingspan 30–38 mm
Day-flying — slow, conspicuous flight visiting flowers, especially knapweed
species.season: Flies June–August. Papery straw-coloured cocoons conspicuous on grass stems. Contains hydrogen cyanide — toxic to predators.

conf.d: Five-spot burnet has 5 red spots (not 6) on each forewing. Requires close inspection — can be difficult to distinguish in the field.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, flower-rich areas. Migratory — arrives from southern Europe. Increasingly common in Denmark.
feat: Hovers in front of flowers while feeding with long proboscis — like a hummingbird
Brown forewings, orange hindwings visible as a blur when hovering
Broad black-and-white tail fan
Wingspan 40–50 mm
Audible humming from wingbeats — often mistaken for an actual hummingbird
species.season: Migrants arrive June–September. Feeds on buddleia, valerian, jasmine. Active in sunshine. Increasingly seen in Danish summers.

species.hab: Meadows, roadsides, waste ground, coastal grassland. Locally common on Sjælland wherever ragwort grows.
feat: Forewings charcoal-black with narrow red stripes and red spots
Hindwings solid red
Caterpillars very conspicuous: orange and black striped, on ragwort
Wingspan 32–42 mm
Day-flying, with weak fluttering flight
species.season: Adults fly May–July. Orange-black caterpillars on ragwort July–August — often easier to spot than the moth. Toxic to predators.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, hedgerows, parks, crops. The classic Danish ladybird. Very common everywhere.
feat: Red wing cases with exactly 7 black spots (3+3+1 shared across the midline)
Black thorax with two white patches
Length 6–8 mm
Both adults and larvae are voracious aphid predators
Hibernates in groups in sheltered spots over winter
species.season: Active March–October. Most conspicuous May–August when aphids are abundant. Congregates before hibernation in autumn.

conf.d: Harlequin ladybird is larger (7–8 mm), extremely variable in pattern (can be red with many spots, black with red spots, or orange). Invasive species.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, buildings, woodland. Invasive species from Asia. Now very common across Denmark. Often enters buildings in autumn.
feat: Extremely variable: red with 0–21 spots, OR black with 2–4 red/orange spots, OR orange variants
Larger than 7-spot ladybird (7–8 mm)
White or cream face with M-shaped or W-shaped black mark on pronotum
Aggregates in huge numbers on buildings in autumn seeking hibernation sites
Outcompetes and preys on native ladybird species
species.season: Active March–November. Massive autumn aggregations on buildings. Has displaced native ladybirds in many areas.

conf.d: Seven-spot is always the same pattern: red with exactly 7 spots, slightly smaller, white pronotum patches. Not variable.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, woodland edges. Fairly common on Sjælland in summer.
feat: Brilliant metallic green or gold-green beetle
Flattened body with small white flecks on wing cases
Length 15–20 mm
Flies clumsily with wing cases closed (unlike most beetles)
Larvae develop in compost heaps and decaying wood
species.season: Adults fly May–August. Found on roses, elderflowers, hogweed umbels. Larvae sometimes found in compost bins — white C-shaped grubs.

species.hab: Meadows, hedgerows, gardens, roadsides. Very common in mid-summer across Sjælland.
feat: Elongated soft-bodied beetle, orange-red with black tips to wing cases
Length 8–10 mm
Often seen in mating pairs on flower heads — hence nickname 'hogweed bonking beetle'
Predatory — feeds on small insects, also visits flowers for pollen
Soft wing cases (not hard like typical beetles)
species.season: Abundant June–August. Swarms on hogweed and other umbellifer flower heads. Very conspicuous.

species.hab: Gardens wherever lilies and fritillaries are grown. Invasive — spreading across Denmark.
feat: Bright scarlet-red wing cases and head, black legs and underside
Length 6–8 mm
Squeaks when picked up (stridulation)
Larvae disguise themselves with their own frass (droppings) — black blobs on lily leaves
Significant garden pest destroying lily foliage and flowers
species.season: Active April–September. Adults overwinter in soil. Check lilies from April onwards for adults and larvae.

conf.d: Firebug is a true bug (not a beetle), flattened, with red and black geometric pattern, found at tree bases not on lilies.

species.hab: Gardens, woodland, hedgerows, under logs and stones. Common across Sjælland.
feat: Large black beetle with violet or purple iridescent sheen on wing case margins
Length 20–30 mm — one of the largest common beetles
Smooth (not ridged) wing cases
Flightless — fused wing cases
Fast-running nocturnal predator of slugs, snails and other invertebrates
species.season: Active April–October, mainly nocturnal. Found under logs, stones, garden debris by day. Valuable garden predator.

species.hab: Old deciduous woodland, parks with old trees, gardens near woodland. Uncommon on Sjælland — declining across Europe. Protected species.
feat: Male: enormous antler-like mandibles — unmistakable
Female: smaller mandibles but still large and powerful jaws
Dark reddish-brown to black, 30–75 mm (males can exceed 70 mm)
Denmark's largest beetle
Larvae develop in decaying tree stumps and roots for 3–7 years
species.season: Adults fly June–August on warm evenings. Males fly searching for females, making a loud buzzing sound. Report sightings — monitored species.

conf.d: Lesser stag beetle is smaller (20–32 mm), all black, with much less prominent mandibles. More common.

species.hab: Everywhere flowers grow. Managed colonies throughout Sjælland plus some feral colonies in tree hollows.
feat: Golden-brown thorax, banded amber-brown abdomen with darker stripes
Length 12–15 mm (workers)
Carries pollen in baskets (corbiculae) on hind legs — visible as yellow lumps
Hairy body but less furry than bumblebees
Only stings once (barbed stinger remains in skin)
species.season: Active March–October. Most visible on warm days April–September. Hive colonies managed by beekeepers year-round.

conf.d: Hoverflies have only 2 wings (bees have 4), short antennae, huge eyes, and cannot sting. They hover — bees don't.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, woodland edges, parks. The commonest Danish bumblebee. Nests underground.
feat: Large furry bumblebee with yellow collar band and yellow band on abdomen
Queen has buff (dirty white/beige) tail — workers have white tails
Length: queens 20–25 mm, workers 12–18 mm
Deep buzzing flight
Nests in old mouse holes and other underground cavities
species.season: Queens emerge February–March (very early). Colonies active until October. One of the first and last bumblebees of the year.

conf.d: Very similar — slightly brighter yellow bands, pure white tail (not buff). Virtually impossible to separate reliably in the field without specimen examination.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, parks, roadsides. Common across Sjælland.
feat: Jet black body with bright orange-red tail — very distinctive
No yellow bands (unlike most bumblebees)
Queens large (20–22 mm), workers smaller (12–16 mm)
Males have yellow facial hair and yellow collar band
Nests in walls, stone piles, underground
species.season: Queens from March. Colonies active until September. Males visible July–August with yellow markings.

conf.d: Cuckoo bee is similar black-and-red but has darker, smoky wings and no pollen baskets. Parasitises red-tailed bumblebee nests.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, hedgerows, woodland edges. Very common on Sjælland.
feat: Entirely ginger-brown thorax — distinctive warm orange-brown colour
Abdomen variably banded brown and darker
Smaller and slimmer than most bumblebees (12–15 mm workers)
Builds nests on or just above ground using moss and grass (cards/combs material)
Long tongue — good at accessing tubular flowers like foxgloves and dead-nettles
species.season: Queens from April. One of the last bumblebees still active in autumn (into October). Long season.

species.hab: Everywhere: gardens, parks, picnic areas, buildings. Nests underground or in cavities. Very common.
feat: Classic yellow and black banding on abdomen
Anchor-shaped or dagger-shaped black mark on face
Length 12–17 mm (workers), queens larger
Narrow waist between thorax and abdomen
Can sting repeatedly (unlike honeybees) — smooth stinger
species.season: Colonies founded by queens in spring. Workers from June. Most aggressive August–September when colony declines and workers seek sugary food. Queens hibernate over winter.

conf.d: German wasp has three black dots on face (not anchor mark). Otherwise very similar in size and behaviour. Both species are common.
Hoverflies are wasp mimics with only 2 wings, cannot sting, and have large eyes. Much smaller head.

species.hab: Woodland, parks, orchards, gardens with old trees. Present on Sjælland but less common than wasps.
feat: Much larger than common wasp — 25–35 mm (queens up to 40 mm)
Reddish-brown thorax and head (not yellow like wasps)
Yellow and brown/dark banding on abdomen
Deep buzzing flight — loud and intimidating but generally not aggressive
Nests in tree hollows, attics, bird boxes
species.season: Colonies active May–November. Attracted to light at night (unlike common wasps). Generally docile unless nest is disturbed. Hunts other insects including wasps.

conf.d: Asian hornet (not yet established in Denmark) has dark brown/black body with single orange band and yellow leg tips. REPORT any sighting immediately — invasive threat to honeybees.

species.hab: Conifer and mixed woodland. Locally common in forests on Sjælland. Protected in some areas.
feat: Large ant (8–10 mm) with reddish-brown thorax and head, dark abdomen
Builds large mound nests from pine needles, twigs, and soil — up to 1 m tall
No sting — sprays formic acid instead (can be smelled near large nests)
Extremely well-organised colonies of up to 500,000 workers
Important woodland ecosystem species — seed dispersal, pest control
species.season: Active March–October. Mound nests visible year-round. Workers forage on tree trunks and forest floor in organised trails.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, parks, anywhere with flowers. The commonest hoverfly in Denmark. Important pollinator.
feat: Orange-yellow abdomen with distinctive double black bands (like marmalade stripes)
Hovers motionless in air, then darts sideways — characteristic hoverfly behaviour
Only 2 wings (not 4 like wasps and bees)
Large compound eyes, short antennae
Length 10–12 mm — much smaller than the wasps they mimic
species.season: Active March–November. Migratory — huge numbers arrive from continental Europe in spring. Larvae eat aphids. Adults pollinate flowers.

conf.d: Wasps have 4 wings, obvious waist, longer antennae, and never hover. Hoverflies have 2 wings, no waist, and hover perfectly still.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, meadows, farmland. Very common. Excellent honeybee mimic.
feat: Convincing honeybee mimic — brown-banded abdomen, furry thorax
But: only 2 wings, short antennae, huge eyes — all signs of a fly
Hovers and visits flowers exactly like a bee
Length 14–18 mm
Larvae (rat-tailed maggots) live in stagnant water — long breathing siphon
species.season: Active March–November. Adults overwinter. One of the first flower visitors in spring. Visits same flowers as bees.

conf.d: Honeybees have 4 wings, longer antennae, pollen baskets on hind legs, and don't hover. Look for the eyes — drone fly has huge bulging eyes meeting on top of head.

species.hab: Gardens, houses, farms, near rubbish and animal waste. Very common everywhere.
feat: Metallic blue-black shiny abdomen — distinctive iridescent blue
Loud buzzing flight
Length 10–14 mm
Black hairy thorax
Attracted to meat, rubbish, and animal droppings — lays eggs on decaying matter
species.season: Active year-round in mild weather, peak spring–autumn. Enters houses frequently. Important decomposer.

conf.d: Greenbottle is metallic green (not blue), slightly smaller, with similar habits.

species.hab: Gardens, lawns, meadows, parks. Very common on Sjælland. Larvae (leatherjackets) live in soil.
feat: Extremely long fragile legs that easily detach
Narrow grey-brown body, 15–25 mm long
V-shaped wing posture at rest
Slow clumsy flight — bounces off walls and ceilings indoors
Often mistaken for a giant mosquito but does NOT bite
species.season: Adults most numerous August–October. Attracted to lights at night. Larvae (leatherjackets) feed on grass roots — can damage lawns.

species.hab: Ponds, lakes, ditches, gardens with water. The commonest dragonfly on Sjælland.
feat: Males: bright red-orange abdomen, brown thorax, yellow-sided
Females/immatures: yellow-brown abdomen
Length 35–44 mm, wingspan 50–60 mm
Perches frequently on vegetation, posts, even people — tame and approachable
Darts out to catch prey then returns to same perch
species.season: Adults June–November (one of the last dragonflies each year). Most common August–October. Often basks on sunny paths and fences.

conf.d: Ruddy darter males are deeper blood-red (not orange-red), with a more club-shaped abdomen and all-black legs (common darter has yellow-striped legs).

species.hab: Lakes, ponds, canals, slow rivers. Common on Sjælland. Patrols over water and along hedgerows.
feat: Large dragonfly — body length 70–77 mm, wingspan up to 100 mm
Entirely brown wings — unique among Danish dragonflies (others have clear wings)
Brown body with blue spots (male) or yellow spots (female)
Powerful tireless flight — patrols territories for long periods
Golden-brown wing tint visible even at distance
species.season: Adults July–October. Often seen hawking insects along woodland edges and hedgerows, sometimes far from water.

conf.d: Southern hawker has clear (not brown) wings, and broad green or blue bands on a black abdomen. Also common and similar size.

species.hab: Large ponds, lakes, gravel pits. Fairly common on Sjælland at larger water bodies.
feat: One of Europe's largest dragonflies — body 66–84 mm, wingspan up to 110 mm
Male: bright sky-blue abdomen with black dorsal line
Female: green abdomen with brown dorsal line
Apple-green thorax
Dominant — aggressively defends territory against all other dragonflies
species.season: Adults June–September. Males patrol over open water. Females oviposit into floating vegetation.

species.hab: Slow-flowing rivers and streams with muddy bottoms. Locally common on Sjælland along suitable waterways.
feat: Male: metallic blue-green body with conspicuous dark blue-black band across each wing
Female: metallic green body with translucent green-tinted wings
Butterfly-like fluttering flight — very different from typical dragonfly dashing
Length 45–48 mm
Damselfly (not dragonfly) — holds wings partly closed at rest
species.season: Adults May–August. Males display over water with slow fluttering flight. One of Denmark's most beautiful insects.

conf.d: Beautiful demoiselle males have entirely dark-coloured wings (no clear areas), and prefer faster-flowing streams. Less common on Sjælland.

species.hab: Still and slow-moving water: ponds, lakes, canals, ditches. Very common on Sjælland — the most abundant damselfly.
feat: Male: bright blue with black markings — mushroom-shaped mark on segment 2
Female: variable — blue, green, or brown forms all occur
Slender body, 29–36 mm long
Holds wings closed along body at rest (damselfly not dragonfly)
Weak fluttering flight low over water and marginal vegetation
species.season: Adults May–September. Enormous numbers around ponds and lakes. Often perches on reeds and floating leaves.

conf.d: Azure damselfly has a U-shaped (not mushroom-shaped) mark on segment 2. Requires close inspection — very similar in the field.

species.hab: Warm sunny spots at bases of lime trees and mallows. Locally common in parks and gardens on Sjælland. Expanding range northward.
feat: Striking red and black geometric pattern on back — unmistakable
Triangular black head, red pronotum with black centre
Flat oval body, 9–11 mm
Gregarious — found in dense clusters of dozens or hundreds
A true bug (Hemiptera) — not a beetle; sucks plant juices
species.season: Active April–October. Congregates in large numbers at tree bases and on warm walls in spring and autumn. Harmless.

conf.d: Rhopalid bug has similar red-and-black coloring but a different pattern, more elongated shape, and is solitary.

species.hab: Gardens, hedgerows, woodland edges, parks. Common on Sjælland.
feat: Bright green shield-shaped body — classic 'stink bug' shape
Turns bronze-brown before hibernation in autumn
Length 12–14 mm
5-segmented antennae
Produces unpleasant smell when handled (stink glands)
species.season: Active April–October. Green in spring/summer, turns brown September–October. Hibernates in leaf litter. Feeds on plant sap.

conf.d: Southern green shield bug is slightly larger with 3 small pale dots at the front of the scutellum. Rare migrant to Denmark.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, under stones, in flowerpots, in fruit, under bark. Very common everywhere. Often enters houses.
feat: Elongated dark brown body with prominent curved pincers (cerci) at rear
Males have strongly curved pincers; females have straighter ones
Length 12–15 mm (body, excluding pincers)
Wings folded under tiny wing cases — can fly but rarely does
Nocturnal — hides in crevices by day
species.season: Active year-round but most visible May–October. Females show remarkable maternal care — guard eggs and young. Despite the name, does not enter ears.

species.hab: Tall grass, hedgerows, scrub, gardens. Fairly common on Sjælland in late summer.
feat: Very large bright green insect — body 28–36 mm plus long ovipositor in females
Extremely long antennae — longer than the body
Brown stripe along top of head and back
Powerful hind legs for jumping
Loud prolonged stridulation (chirping) on warm evenings — sounds like sewing machine
species.season: Adults July–October. Song audible from dusk. Mainly carnivorous — catches other insects. Can deliver a sharp bite if handled.

conf.d: Grasshoppers are much smaller, have short antennae (shorter than body), and produce brief chirps (not prolonged songs).

species.hab: Dry grassland, meadows, roadsides, gardens, dunes. Common on Sjælland.
feat: Compact brown or greenish-brown body, 15–22 mm
Short antennae — shorter than body (key: grasshopper vs cricket)
Large hind legs for jumping
Short buzzing chirps produced by rubbing hind legs against forewings
Variable colour: brown, green, purple, or combinations
species.season: Adults July–October. Song is a brief buzzy chirp repeated every few seconds. Jumps powerfully when disturbed. Flies short distances.

conf.d: Bush-crickets are larger, have very long antennae (longer than body), and produce prolonged continuous song.

species.hab: Gardens, hedgerows, woodland edges, around buildings. Very common across Sjælland. Not an insect — an arachnid.
feat: White cross-shaped marking on abdomen — the 'diadem'
Colour variable: yellow-brown, orange-brown, or dark brown, but cross always visible
Female body 10–15 mm, males much smaller (5–8 mm)
Builds classic orb web up to 40 cm across, often across paths at head height
8 legs (not 6 — arachnid, not insect)
species.season: Most conspicuous August–October when females are large and webs are everywhere. Males seen wandering in autumn seeking mates. Dies after first hard frost.
